{"url": "https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=all%3Apath+dependence+reinforcement+learning+memory+preference+formation&max_results=4", "scope": "paper abstracts; preprints, peer-review status not verified", "excerpt": "title: The Open Ant: A Robot Platform for Reinforcement Learning Research
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18488v1
published: 2026-07-20T20:18:29Z
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) research has demonstrated success in both physical and simulated domains; however, the predominant methodology remains rooted in simulations. The predominance of simulations makes translating research to physical reality uncertain for both algorithms and researchers. We propose a physical platform that is designed to simplify the transition. In this paper, we present the Open Ant: a physical variant of the commonly used Gymnasium Ant environment, along with a simulation. We demonstrate that competent walking policies can be learned from scratch in approximately one hour directly from the physical robot's experience for two substantially different RL algorithms: SARSA($λ$) and Soft Actor-Critic (SAC). Separately, we show policies that were learned in simulation transfer to reality. We also examine how well the platform supports a nimble experimental ecosystem. Specifically, we observe the speed with which new users from diverse backgrounds achieve their first success with the platform, and how easily the platform can be repaired and updated when hardware issues arise. Both the hardware design and software are available as open-source on GitHub for ease of customization. In summary, we advocate for the use of the Open Ant for RL researchers who frequently use simulated environments, so they can more easily include robot experiments in their evaluations.

{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=computational+models+of+autonomous+goal+formation+and+objective+discovery&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Towards Intelligent Membrane Systems: A Critical Analysis of Digital Twin-ML Integration for Real-Time Process Optimization, Fouling Management, and Autonomous Design.\", \"abstract\": \"Membrane separation is central to potable water production, wastewater reclamation, desalination, gas separation, and decarbonization, yet its economics remain constrained by fouling and by a gap between process data and timely operating decisions. Digital twins (DTs) offer live, bidirectionally coupled virtual representations of physical assets, while machine learning (ML) extracts predictive and prescriptive insights from operational data. Together, they are promising computational approaches for membrane systems. However, their applications have largely evolved independently across fouling prediction, DT development, and ML-based materials discovery. This review argues that these are converging strands of a single trajectory toward self-sensing, self-predicting, and eventually self-designing membrane systems, and that treating them separately obscures key interdependencies. The contributions are threefold. First, applying the digital model/digital shadow/digital twin taxonomy, it shows that most published membrane DTs are digital shadows (DSs). Second, it proposes a five-level autonomy framework, inspired by vehicle automation taxonomies, providing a unified scale for comparing applications ranging from LSTM-based fouling forecasting and reinforcement learning dosing control to autonomous materials laboratories. Third, it integrates autonomous materials design, including self-driving laboratories, inverse design, generative models, and Bayesian search, into the upper levels of this ladder. Evidence is synthesized across reverse osmosis, nanofiltration, ultrafiltration, microfiltration, membrane bioreactors, membrane distillation, and gas separation membranes, with emphasis on critically assessing model performance and generalizability. The study concludes with a roadmap for overcoming data limitations, poor interpretability, interoperability gaps, cybersecurity risks, techno-eco…

{"url": "https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=all%3Aevaluating+failure+modes+of+open-ended+curiosity+and+hypothesis+generation+in+autonomous+agents&max_results=4", "scope": "paper abstracts; preprints, peer-review status not verified", "excerpt": "title: ARTPS: Depth-Enhanced Hybrid Anomaly Detection and Learnable Curiosity Score for Autonomous Rover Target Prioritization
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2509.00042v1
published: 2025-08-23T17:37:05Z
summary: We present ARTPS (Autonomous Rover Target Prioritization System), a novel hybrid AI system that combines depth estimation, anomaly detection, and learnable curiosity scoring for autonomous exploration of planetary surfaces. Our approach integrates monocular depth estimation using Vision Transformers with multi-component anomaly detection and a weighted curiosity score that balances known value, anomaly signals, depth variance, and surface roughness. The system achieves state-of-the-art performance with AUROC of 0.94, AUPRC of 0.89, and F1-Score of 0.87 on Mars rover datasets. We demonstrate significant improvements in target prioritization accuracy through ablation studies and provide comprehensive analysis of component contributions. The hybrid fusion approach reduces false positives by 23% while maintaining high detection sensitivity across diverse terrain types.

title: DeFA: Dependency-Guided Failure Attribution for LLM Agents
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01256v1
published: 2026-10-01T07:50:22Z
summary: Errors in LLM agent executions and their visible consequences can be separated by many steps, making decisive-error localization a matter of understanding both step content and step dependencies. We introduce DeFA, a dependency-guided framework for agent failure attribution. DeFA first combines protocol relations and semantic dependencies into an event dependency graph spanning the trajectory. It then identifies events that may violate task requirements and traces their sources and subsequent effects to construct a failure propagation graph. Finally, DeFA uses step evidence and the steps' roles in failure propagation to identify the decisive error, responsible agent, and error category.
